03.01.title: Functions of several variables
03.01.html:
Real quantities depend on more than one thing. Gas pressure depends on temperature and volume; the stress in a beam depends on position along it and across it; the temperature of a plate depends on x, y and time. This lesson sets up the language: level sets to see such functions, partial derivatives to measure them, and the total differential to estimate how errors and changes combine.

Seeing a function of two variables

f(x,y) is a surface over the plane. Two views help:

  • Level sets (contours): the curves f(x,y)=c. A weather map’s isobars, a topographic map’s height lines, isotherms on a heated plate.
  • Slices: hold one variable fixed and plot f against the other. A slice is an ordinary one-variable function.

Partial derivatives

The partial derivative with respect to x is the slope of the slice in the x direction, with y held fixed:

∂x∂f​(x,y)=h→0lim​hf(x+h,y)−f(x,y)​.

Compute it by treating every other variable as a constant. Numerically, use the central difference from lesson 01.03 in one variable at a time.

The total differential

If both inputs change a little, the changes add up to first order:

df=∂x∂f​dx+∂y∂f​dy.

This is the tangent-plane approximation, the 2D version of the tangent line. Two uses dominate engineering:

  1. Sensitivity: which input matters most? Compare ∣∂f/∂xi​∣Δxi​ term by term.
  2. Error propagation: for independent random errors σi​, σf​≈∑i​(∂f/∂xi​)2σi2​​.

Order of differentiation

For smooth functions, ∂2f/∂x∂y=∂2f/∂y∂x (Schwarz’s theorem). The code checks it numerically.

Worked examplePressure in a heated tank

1 kg of air (R=287 J/(kg K)) at T=300 K in V=0.5 m³. Ideal gas: p=mRT/V=172.2 kPa.

  1. ∂p/∂T=mR/V=574 Pa/K.
  2. ∂p/∂V=−mRT/V2=−344400 Pa/m³.
  3. The tank warms by 2 K and bulges by 0.01 m³: dp=574⋅2−344400⋅0.01=1148−3444=−2296 Pa.
  4. Exact: p(302,0.51)−p(300,0.5)=169949−172200=−2251 Pa. The linear estimate is 2% off because dV/V=2% isn’t tiny.
  5. Error propagation: with σT​=0.5 K and σV​=0.002 m³, σp​=(574⋅0.5)2+(344400⋅0.002)2​=2872+6892​=746 Pa. The volume measurement dominates, so that’s the one to improve.

Exercise 1Which measurement matters?

The bending stress in a rectangular beam is σ=6M/(bh2). With M=2 kN m, b=40 mm, h=100 mm, each measured with 1% error, which dimension dominates the uncertainty in σ?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. σ=6⋅2×106/(40⋅1002)=30 MPa.
  2. Relative sensitivities: ∂M∂σ​σM​=1, ∂b∂σ​σb​=−1, ∂h∂σ​σh​=−2.
  3. 1% errors become 1%, 1% and 2% in σ; combined 1+1+4​=2.4%, about 0.73 MPa.
  4. The depth h dominates because it appears squared. Measure it more carefully first.

03.02.title: The gradient
03.02.html:
The gradient packs all the partial derivatives into one vector, and that vector has a meaning you can see: it points uphill, as steeply as possible, perpendicular to the contours. Heat flows against the temperature gradient, fluid accelerates down the pressure gradient, and optimisers walk against the gradient of the cost. This lesson builds all three ideas from one formula.

Definition and directional derivatives

∇f=(∂x∂f​,∂y∂f​,∂z∂f​).

The rate of change of f in the direction of a unit vector u is the directional derivative

Du​f=∇f⋅u=∣∇f∣cosθ.

It’s largest when u points along ∇f (rate ∣∇f∣), zero when u is perpendicular to it (moving along a contour), and most negative straight against it.

Gradients in physics

  • Fourier’s law: heat flux q=−k∇T. Heat runs downhill in temperature, fastest where the isotherms crowd together.
  • Pressure force: a fluid parcel feels −∇p per unit volume.
  • Conservative forces: F=−∇V for a potential energy V (more in lesson 03.07).

Gradient descent

To minimise f, step against the gradient: xk+1​=xk​−η∇f(xk​). For the quadratic bowl f=21​xTAx, the gradient is Ax and each step multiplies the error in eigen-direction i by 1−ηλi​. So:

  • The step must satisfy η<2/λmax​, or the steepest direction blows up.
  • With the best fixed step, the error shrinks by κ+1κ−1​ per step, where κ=λmax​/λmin​. Long, narrow valleys (large κ) make gradient descent zigzag and crawl.

That’s the same condition number from Phase 02, and it’s why CG (lesson 02.15) and Newton’s method (03.03) beat plain descent.

Worked exampleHeat flow on a plate

A plate has temperature T(x,y)=100−2x2−y2 °C, with x,y in metres, and conductivity k=50 W/(m K).

  1. ∇T=(−4x,−2y). At (1,2): ∇T=(−4,−4) °C/m.
  2. Rate of change heading in direction (3,4)/5: Du​T=−4⋅0.6−4⋅0.8=−5.6 °C/m.
  3. Steepest increase: along (−1,−1)/2​, towards the hot centre, at ∣∇T∣=42​=5.66 °C/m.
  4. Heat flux: q=−k∇T=(200,200) W/m², magnitude 283 W/m², pointing away from the centre.
  5. Check perpendicularity: the isotherm through (1,2) is 2x2+y2=6, with tangent direction (−y,2x)=(−2,2). Its dot product with ∇T=(−4,−4) is 8−8=0.

Exercise 1The fastest way down

A hill has height z=300−0.002x2−0.001y2 m. At the point (100,200), in which direction does water run, and how steep is the slope there in percent?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ∇z=(−0.004x,−0.002y)=(−0.4,−0.4).
  2. Water runs along −∇z=(0.4,0.4), that is towards (1,1)/2​, away from the summit.
  3. Slope =∣∇z∣=0.42​=0.566, a 56.6% grade (about 29.5∘). Steep: that’s a black ski run.

03.03.title: Multivariable Taylor and the Hessian
03.03.html:
Near a point, a smooth function of several variables looks like a constant plus a tilted plane plus a curved bowl, saddle or dome. The tilt is the gradient; the curvature is the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives. Its eigenvalues tell you whether a stationary point is a minimum, maximum or saddle, which is exactly the stability test for equilibria in mechanics.

The second-order expansion

f(x+h)≈f(x)+∇f(x)⋅h+21​hTH(x)h,Hij​=∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​.

H is symmetric for smooth f (lesson 03.01), so the spectral theorem (02.10) applies: in the eigenvector directions, the quadratic term is a sum of independent parabolas 21​λi​ci2​.

Classifying stationary points

At a stationary point ∇f=0, and the Hessian decides:

Eigenvalues of H Shape Type
all positive bowl local minimum
all negative dome local maximum
mixed signs saddle neither
some zero flat direction the test is inconclusive

In mechanics, an equilibrium is stable when the potential energy has a minimum there: H positive definite (lesson 02.11). A ball on a saddle-shaped surface is in equilibrium but unstable.

Newton’s method in several variables

Minimise the quadratic model instead of f: set its gradient to zero, ∇f+Hh=0, and solve for the step

Hh=−∇f.

Near a minimum with positive definite H, this converges quadratically, like the 1D Newton method in lesson 01.05, and it doesn’t care how elongated the bowl is. The cost is forming and solving with H each step.

Worked exampleFind and classify

f(x,y)=x3−3x+y2.

  1. ∇f=(3x2−3, 2y)=0 at (1,0) and (−1,0).
  2. H=(6x0​02​).
  3. At (1,0): eigenvalues 6 and 2, both positive, so a minimum with f=−2.
  4. At (−1,0): eigenvalues −6 and 2, a saddle with f=2. It’s a maximum along x and a minimum along y.
  5. Quadratic model at the minimum: f≈−2+3(x−1)2+y2. At (1.1,0.1) it gives −1.960; the exact value is 1.331−3.3+0.01=−1.959.

Exercise 1Stability of a spring-loaded hinge

A bar of length L hinged at its base is held upright by a torsional spring kt​ and loaded by a vertical force P at its tip. The potential energy is V(θ)=21​kt​θ2+PLcosθ. When is the upright position θ=0 stable?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. V′(θ)=kt​θ−PLsinθ, which is zero at θ=0: an equilibrium for every load.
  2. V′′(0)=kt​−PL.
  3. Stable (a minimum) when kt​−PL>0, so P<kt​/L. The critical load Pcr​=kt​/L is a buckling load, the 1D version of the Euler column in Phase 06.
  4. Above it, V′′(0)<0: the upright position becomes a maximum and the bar tips over to a bent equilibrium.

03.04.title: Constrained optimisation
03.04.html:
Design is optimisation with rules: the lightest bracket that doesn’t yield, the cheapest tank that holds 1000 litres, the strongest beam that fits in a given depth. Lagrange multipliers turn “optimise f subject to g=0” into a system of equations, and the multiplier itself has a meaning engineers use constantly: the price of the constraint.

The geometric condition

At a constrained optimum you can’t improve f by sliding along the constraint curve g=0. So the gradient of f has no component along the curve: it’s perpendicular to it, just like ∇g. The two gradients are parallel:

∇f=λ∇g,g(x)=0.

Equivalently, look for stationary points of the Lagrangian L(x,λ)=f(x)−λg(x) in all variables, x and λ together.

What the multiplier means

If the constraint is g(x)=c and you relax c a little, the optimal value changes at the rate

dcdf∗​=λ.

That’s a shadow price: how much more performance you’d buy per unit of loosened constraint. In mechanics, multipliers are the reaction forces: minimise energy subject to “this node doesn’t move”, and λ is the support force.

Inequalities

Real constraints are often inequalities (σ≤σallow​). The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions extend Lagrange: either the constraint is inactive and its multiplier is zero, or it’s active and behaves like an equality. Lesson 04.19 builds a solver for them.

Worked exampleThe cheapest can

Make a closed cylinder holding V=1 litre with the least sheet metal. Area A=2πr2+2πrh; constraint πr2h=V.

  1. ∂A/∂r=4πr+2πh=λ2πrh and ∂A/∂h=2πr=λπr2.
  2. The second equation gives λ=2/r. Substitute into the first: 4πr+2πh=4πh, so h=2r. The height equals the diameter.
  3. With V=10−3 m³: 2πr3=V gives r=54.19 mm and h=108.4 mm.
  4. Area: A=6πr2=0.05536 m² =553.6 cm².
  5. Multiplier: λ=2/r=36.9 m⁻¹. One more millilitre (10−6 m³) costs 36.9×10−6 m² =0.37 cm² of extra sheet.

Real cans are taller than this because the lids are thicker, seamed, and more expensive per area than the wall. Put that cost into A and the optimum shifts.

Exercise 1The strongest beam from a log

A rectangular beam of width b and depth h is cut from a round log of diameter D, so b2+h2=D2. Bending strength is proportional to the section modulus bh2/6. Find the best ratio h/b.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Maximise bh2 subject to b2+h2=D2. Lagrange: h2=2λb and 2bh=2λh, so λ=b and h2=2b2.
  2. h/b=2​≈1.41.
  3. From the constraint: b=D/3​=0.577D and h=2/3​D=0.816D.
  4. This is the classic result Parent derived in 1708, and close to the proportions of standard sawn timber joists.

quiz.q: Optimal can radius in mm for V=0.5 litre (closed cylinder, minimum area).
quiz.explain: r=(V/2π)1/3.

Perpendicular to ∇g

03.05.title: Double and triple integrals
03.05.html:
Mass, centroid, second moment of area, total heat in a body: all are integrals over a region in 2D or 3D. You compute them as iterated one-dimensional integrals, slicing the region into strips. The second moment of area I is the headline example in mechanics, because it sets how stiff a beam is in bending.

Iterated integrals

Over a rectangle, integrate in one variable with the other fixed, then integrate the result:

∬R​fdA=∫ab​(∫cd​f(x,y)dy)dx.

For a non-rectangular region, the inner limits depend on the outer variable: for the region between y=g1​(x) and y=g2​(x), the inner integral runs from g1​(x) to g2​(x). Fubini’s theorem says the order doesn’t matter for well-behaved f, so pick whichever makes the limits easiest.

Quantities you’ll compute

Quantity Integral
Area A=∬dA
Centroid yˉ​=A1​∬ydA
Second moment about the x axis Ix​=∬y2dA
Mass of a body m=∭ρdV

For a rectangle of width b and height h about its centroid, I=∫−h/2h/2​by2dy=bh3/12. The cube on h is why beams are deep rather than wide.

The parallel axis theorem

The second moment about an axis a distance d from the centroid is I=Ic​+Ad2. Build composite sections (T, I, channel) from rectangles with it.

Numerical integration in 2D

The midpoint rule extends directly: split the region into cells, evaluate at each centre, sum value × area. Its error is O(h2) as in 1D. For high dimensions, grids become hopeless (nd points) and Monte Carlo (average f at random points) wins: its error falls like 1/N​ regardless of dimension.

Worked exampleBending stiffness of a T-beam

Flange 100×20 mm on top of a web 20×80 mm, base at y=0.

  1. Areas: flange 2000 mm² with centroid at y=90; web 1600 mm² at y=40.
  2. Centroid: yˉ​=(2000⋅90+1600⋅40)/3600=67.78 mm.
  3. Flange: Ic​=100⋅203/12=66667, distance d=22.22, Ad2=987654. Total 1054321 mm⁴.
  4. Web: Ic​=20⋅803/12=853333, d=27.78, Ad2=1234568. Total 2087901 mm⁴.
  5. I=3.142×106 mm⁴. The code gets the same number by brute-force double integration over the shape.

A solid 40×100 mm rectangle (more material, 4000 mm²) has I=40⋅1003/12=3.333×106 mm⁴. The T uses 10% less material for 6% less stiffness, and its flange can carry a slab.

Exercise 1Wide or deep?

A plank is 200×50 mm. Compare its second moment of area laid flat (bending about the axis parallel to the 200 mm side) and on edge. By what factor is the on-edge orientation stiffer?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Flat: b=200, h=50: I=200⋅503/12=2.083×106 mm⁴.
  2. On edge: b=50, h=200: I=50⋅2003/12=3.333×107 mm⁴.
  3. Ratio (200/50)2=16. Same material, sixteen times stiffer, because the depth is cubed and the width only enters linearly.

quiz.explain: bh3/12=30⋅216000/12.
